items.question: Does gold-ness remain exclusive to a lump and absent in a crown or other forms?
premises: Gold-ness is present in a lump of gold.
A crown and similar objects are also made of gold.
Essential nature does not vanish with change of form.
items.inference: Gold-ness cannot be denied in the crown merely because it appears in a different form.
items.plain_english: If gold-ness were present only in a lump of gold and not in a crown and the like, that would be mistaken.

items.question: What determines whether an accusation of transgression is valid in honoring something?
premises: Honoring involves recognizing what is truly present.
An accusation of transgression depends on a correct determination.
Misrecognition can lead to a false charge of violation.
items.inference: The validity of a transgression charge depends on rightly determining the underlying reality.
uncertainties: The exact ritual or social context of satkṛtau is not specified.
items.plain_english: In honoring, what must be determined is whether the accusation of transgression is justified.

rows.grounds: refers to the reality in question

items.question: Does the ongoing manifestation of that reality require the arising of an external cause?
premises: The reality in question continues to proceed or manifest.
An external cause would imply dependence on something else.
If its nature is intrinsic, no new cause needs to arise.
items.inference: In such proceeding, there is no arising of an external cause for it.
items.plain_english: Thus, in its ongoing manifestation, there is no arising of an external cause for it.

items.question: Why would a supposed cause abandon its own form to produce an effect?
premises: A cause is proposed to explain manifestation.
Abandoning its form would undermine its causal identity.
A coherent account of causality must explain this change.
items.inference: The claim of causality is problematic if it requires the cause to abandon its own form.
items.plain_english: It must be explained: why would causality require something to abandon its own form?

items.question: What follows if everything is established as having the nature of the triad of powers?
premises: The triad of powers defines a fundamental nature.
Everything may be said to be established in that nature.
If so, no thing stands outside this triadic constitution.
items.inference: All things share the established nature of the triad of powers.
uncertainties: The specific three powers are not named in this verse.
items.plain_english: Where everything is established as having the nature of the triad of powers.

items.question: How can something appear to have that nature if it does not truly possess it?
premises: A thing may lack a certain nature in reality.
Yet it may appear to have that nature.
Such a discrepancy invites critical questioning.
items.inference: If appearance diverges from reality, an objection arises about how that appearance is possible.
items.plain_english: If, in the absence of that nature, such an appearance occurs, then an objection is raised.

items.question: On what basis is Śiva-ness described as present in both peaceful and gross states?
premises: Śiva-ness is affirmed in the peaceful state.
Śiva-ness is also affirmed in the gross state.
A common basis must justify this universal attribution.
items.inference: The teaching asserts Śiva-ness across both subtle and gross states.
items.plain_english: Where Śiva-ness is described as present in the peaceful and also in the gross.

rows.grounds: union of the three powers in that form

items.question: Is the union of the triad of powers the true reality underlying all states?
premises: Reality is being defined in terms of a union of powers.
The triad of powers was previously identified as fundamental.
If this union is real, it grounds the states described.
items.inference: True reality consists in the union of the triad of powers as described.
items.plain_english: If this is reality, it is the union of the triad of powers in that form.

rows.grounds: endowed with will and other powers

items.question: Why is every thing identified as Śiva possessing consciousness and the powers of will and others?
premises: Śiva is of the nature of consciousness.
Śiva possesses will and the other powers.
All things are grounded in this conscious, powerful reality.
items.inference: Every thing is Śiva, as consciousness endowed with will and the other powers.
items.plain_english: Thus every thing is Śiva, whose form is consciousness and who possesses will and the other powers.

items.question: Can a state like a flame lack the character of action and knowledge?
premises: A flame is taken as an example of a manifest state.
An objection suggests such a state may lack action and knowledge.
If all is Śiva's nature, these powers should be present.
items.inference: The objection claims that in such a state action and knowledge-form are absent.
items.plain_english: Then, in a flame and the like, is that state not of the nature of action and knowledge?

items.question: Does Śiva remain established even in the state being questioned?
premises: The previous verse questioned the presence of powers in a given state.
Śiva is claimed to be present in all states.
If Śiva abides there, that state cannot be devoid of his nature.
items.inference: If Śiva is established in that state, the objection loses its force.
items.plain_english: If that Śiva is established and present in this state.

items.question: Can any existence remain if it is entirely devoid of knowledge and power?
premises: Knowledge and power are essential to Śiva's nature.
A state without knowledge is being considered.
Existence without any power would be untenable.
items.inference: No existence can stand as entirely devoid of power and knowledge.
items.plain_english: Or, in what is without knowledge, it must be known that no existence is without any power.

rows.grounds: in the doctrine of recognition of the Lord

items.question: Where is this principle of universal Śiva-nature investigated in detail?
premises: The preceding verses argue for Śiva's presence in all states.
This doctrine requires systematic investigation.
The Recognition of the Lord is a key source for this inquiry.
items.inference: The matter is investigated in the Īśvarapratyabhijñā.
items.plain_english: Thus, this is investigated in the Īśvarapratyabhijñā.

items.question: How can mutual variety belong to Śiva while remaining his very nature?
premises: Śiva's nature is being affirmed as universal.
Phenomena appear as mutually varied.
This variety must be accounted for within Śiva's nature.
items.inference: The mutual variety of things is itself the nature of Śiva.
items.plain_english: The mutual variety that exists is the very nature of Śiva.

items.question: How should the claim that all is Śiva-natured be explained in what follows?
premises: All things have been identified with Śiva's nature.
This claim needs further explanation.
The explanation will be given in the subsequent discussion.
items.inference: The way all is Śiva-natured is to be stated further on.
items.plain_english: How all is of the nature of Śiva is to be explained hereafter.

items.question: Will the explanation of all things being Śiva-natured be provided later?
premises: The previous verse promised an explanation.
A future statement is indicated.
The teaching unfolds progressively.
items.inference: The explanation will indeed be given later.
items.plain_english: Thus it will be explained later.

items.question: Can a pot be said to be merely a pot and nothing more in this framework?
premises: A pot is a common example of a limited object.
One might claim it is only what it appears to be.
The doctrine asserts a deeper Śiva-nature in all things.
items.inference: The challenge is to state whether the pot is only such and not Śiva-natured.
items.plain_english: Let it be said here: is a pot merely of that such kind alone?

items.question: Whose power constitutes the entire range of arisen categories?
premises: All categories of things have arisen.
Power is the source of manifestation.
The supreme deity is identified as the possessor of this power.
items.inference: The entire range of arisen categories is the power of the God of gods.
items.plain_english: The entire power of all arisen categories belongs to the God of gods.

items.question: What scriptural authority supports the unity and supremacy of Rudra?
premises: The doctrine affirms a single supreme reality.
Scriptural revelation is cited as support.
Rudra is named as that one supreme being.
items.inference: Revelation states that Rudra is one and supreme.
uncertainties: The specific śruti passage is indicated only by itītyādi.
items.plain_english: In revelation it is said, 'Rudra is one,' and so on, and he is supreme.

items.question: Can something unreal have established existence as a subsidiary part of an injunction?
premises: An injunction may require subsidiary elements.
Subsidiary status presupposes some reality or validity.
What is unreal cannot function as a genuine subsidiary.
items.inference: If existence is only as a subsidiary to injunction, the unreal cannot be established as such a subsidiary.
items.plain_english: If existence is claimed only as a subsidiary to an injunction, what is unreal cannot be established as a subsidiary.

items.question: Who has demonstrated the principle that the unreal cannot serve as a valid subsidiary?
premises: The previous verse stated a principle about unreality and subsidiarity.
This principle has been demonstrated by a known school.
The followers of Jaimini are cited as authorities.
items.inference: The followers of Jaimini have shown this principle.
items.plain_english: This has been shown by the followers of Jaimini.

rows.grounds: the pair of bondage and liberation
because of the nature of Śiva

items.question: Why do bondage and liberation not ultimately differ when viewed from Śiva-ness?
premises: Bondage and liberation are ordinarily distinguished.
All reality is grounded in Śiva-ness.
From the standpoint of Śiva-ness, ultimate difference collapses.
items.inference: Bondage and liberation do not truly differ everywhere because of Śiva-ness.
items.plain_english: Bondage and liberation do not differ at all, because of Śiva-ness everywhere.

rows.grounds: from which bondage and liberation arise

items.question: How are the world-cycle and the states of bondage and liberation grounded in the same power?
premises: The same divine power underlies all manifestation.
The world-cycle is a manifestation of that power.
Bondage and liberation are states within that manifestation.
items.inference: That very power is the world-cycle, and from it the states of bondage and liberation are established.
items.plain_english: That very power is this world-cycle, and from it the states of bondage and liberation are established.

rows.grounds: the pair of bondage and liberation

items.question: In what sense are bondage and liberation both characterized as forms of ignorance?
premises: Bondage and liberation were said to be established states.
From the standpoint of Śiva-ness they do not ultimately differ.
Their apparent distinction rests on ignorance.
items.inference: Thus bondage and liberation, as established states, are both of the form of ignorance.
items.plain_english: Thus, as established states, bondage and liberation are both of the form of ignorance.
